newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaitis welcome reported bid to oust Saddam.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaitis welcome reported bid to oust Saddam.

text.p: Delighted Kuwaitis on Sunday welcomed reports that U.S. intelligence had plotted to overthrow their former occupier, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

Still traumatised by their seven-month experience of Baghdad's rule in 1990-91, Kuwaitis expressed hope the reported Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) programme would survive fresh turmoil in northern Iraq.
"The execution of Saddam Hussein is a precondition for any peace for mankind," said Youssef al-Sultan, asssistant director general of the Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research.
"His (ruling) Baath party does not sleep happily by night unless it has produced a lake of blood by day."

Political scientist and candidate in parliamentary elections Abdul-Redha Assiri said: "For us Kuwaitis anything that would undermine the Iraqi regime is a good omen. It releases us of a burden and a psychological load and will save the area from a tyrant."

The Washington Post reported on Sunday that Saddam's assault in late August against Kurds in northern Iraq undermined a covert operation by the CIA aimed at overthrowing the Iraqi leader and led to the arrest and execution of 100 Iraqis associated with the effort.
The New York Times on Saturday reported that a handful of CIA officers overseeing the effort in northern Iraq had fled last week as Iraqi forces occupied the city of Arbil.

U.S. President Bill Clinton expanded the covert operation in January, signing a secret order directing the CIA to provide weapons, organise some military training and install some intelligence-gathering equipment for the fractious group seeking to unseat Saddam, officials told the Times.
Iraq occupied Kuwait in 1990-91 after months of disuputes over oil policy, the border and aid. A U.S.-led alliance based in Saudi Arabia ousted Iraqi troops in February 1991.

Member of parliament Abdul-Mohsen Jamal, a frequent critic of American policy in the Middle East, said the task of overthrowing Saddam was so important that it was acceptable for Iraqis to cooperate with any force to achieve that goal.
"The only reason we need for the removal of Saddam Hussein is the suffering of the Iraqi people and the need to instal a democracy in the place of his regime," he said.

"Some people say we need to keep Iraq united, to keep a counterbalance to Iran and we shouldn't topple him until we have a successor. But he in fact should be removed because of the bad human rights situation in Iraq, where conditions of life are less than zero."
Civil servant Saud al-Ajmi voiced a dissenting view, saying the toppling of Saddam would leave a power vacuum in Iraq that would be exploited by neighbouring Iran.

"We like the angel of death better than Saddam Hussein, but Iran's containment, which was a factor that prevented his overthrow in 1991, is now an even bigger reason (to keep Saddam Hussein in power)," he said.
